title: France Opens Diesel Reserves: TotalEnergies and E. Leclerc Slash Fuel Prices Sharply
text:

Leclerc Slash Fuel Prices Sharply
 Add preferred source France has released ten million barrels of diesel from its strategic reserves. The volumes, sold at 0.28 euros per liter instead of around 1.10 euros, are driving noticeable price cuts at the pumps: TotalEnergies lowered the cap at its Access stations to 2.15 euros per liter, while E. Leclerc and Coopérative U announced a discount of 21 cents per liter. The average diesel price recently stood at around 2.37 euros. The backdrop is a strained supply situation with shortages at roughly every seventh station, caused by low Rhine water levels and heavy demand. Key Elements 
 TotalEnergies E. Leclerc Coopérative U Sébastien Lecornu France diesel price strategic reserves Intermarché Dominique Schelcher Thierry Cotillard Following the release of ten million barrels of diesel from France's strategic reserves, the first major fuel retail chains are passing the lower costs on to customers. TotalEnergies, E. Leclerc and Coopérative U announced price cuts at their French pumps over the weekend. The trigger was the regulation published at the end of October, through which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu enabled the opening of state stockpiles.
 TotalEnergies already lowered the price at its roughly 705 Access stations to a maximum of 2.15 euros per liter of diesel as of October 31. That is ten cents below the previous cap of 2.25 euros, which the company has voluntarily maintained at its roughly 3,300 French stations since mid-September. According to the company, Access stations account for around 60 percent of fuel sales in France. Starting Monday, November 2, the new maximum price will also apply at the group's remaining stations, excluding highway locations. The reduction is provisional: TotalEnergies said it will continue to monitor international markets.
 The group justified the move by saying it did not want to wait for the physical delivery of the strategic diesel reserves "in order to give its customers access to these stocks at historic costs." The average diesel price in France stood at around 2.37 euros per liter on Saturday, according to an analysis of 8,842 stations.
 The E. Leclerc retail chain announced a reduction of 21 cents per liter at its roughly 742 French stations. The discount is deducted daily from the respective current market price, the company said. For a 50-liter tank, that translates into savings of a little more than ten euros. The Coopérative U group announced an identical reduction.
 Provider Stations (approx.) Reduction New Price / Discount 
 TotalEnergies (Access) 705 10 cents max. 2.15 euros per liter 
 TotalEnergies (remaining, from November 2) around 3,300 total 10 cents max. 2.15 euros per liter 
 E. Leclerc 742 21 cents discount on daily price 
 Coopérative U n/a 21 cents discount on daily price 
 The average diesel price stood at around 2.37 euros per liter on Saturday; TotalEnergies' Access stations were already below that level.
 The released volumes were purchased before the war in the Middle East and are being sold at 0.28 euros per liter, compared with an average of 1.10 euros per liter in mid-October. Lecornu had expected the measure to bring a price reduction of an estimated 12 to 18 cents per liter. The reduction from E. Leclerc thus exceeds the original expectation.
 The other major chains have so far acted inconsistently. Coopérative U chief Dominique Schelcher had held out the prospect in mid-October of price cuts of "up to 18 cents" starting November 1, depending on transport costs. Thierry Cotillard, president of the Mousquetaires (Intermarché), promised to pass on the reduction without specifying a date or amount. A decree also obliges the stations to display the amount of the price reduction "clearly."
 The measure is driven by a strained supply situation. Around 15 percent of France's nearly 9,900 fuel stations were recently affected by shortages, with at least one fuel product missing at roughly every seventh station. The causes are considered to be the low water level of the Rhine, which is delaying transport, especially in the eastern parts of the country, as well as heavy demand at low-priced stations.
 For consumers, the combination of state reserves and competition among the chains means noticeable relief at the pump. Whether the reductions will last depends on the development of international diesel prices; TotalEnergies has explicitly made the price development provisional. For the market, the key questions are how quickly the other providers follow suit and whether the released volumes will be sufficient to ease the supply bottlenecks through the end of January.
